The factors causing the different responses for the two formation types were studied so that acid-job limit predictions can be extrapolated to other formations. Various post-test core analysis methods were used to study the effects of acid jobs on proppant-embedded fracture face. Comparison of these results with those from intermediate UCS/intermediate porosity core support that the higher UCS core from the current study experienced minor changes after 8-acid cycles.

records.title: Accurate Measurement of Relative Permeability as Crucial Step for Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage: Case Study
records.summary: Abstract Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage is one of the key technologies that can help meet the goal of reducing carbon emissions in the atmosphere by pulling out CO2 emissions from different industries. CO2 storage can provide a way to continue using hydrocarbons while minimizing their environmental impact, making the process valuable for the energy transition. To implement a CO2 storage project, it is necessary to meet existing regulatory framework for planning, implementation, and monitoring, which includes the evaluation of rock-fluid properties. These properties are necessary to ensure that the selected geological formation is suitable for long-term CO2 storage, to predict the CO2 movement through the reservoir during the life of the process, to anticipate changes in the rock, to monitor the evolution of the CO2 and make sure that its injection is efficient and safe. This study was performed aimed to measure CO2-brine relative permeability as one of the most complex rock-fluid properties to comply with current CCUS regulations. In this study, the experimental results of the relative permeability measurements performed in core plugs from a well located in the Gulf of Mexico and six synthetic sandstones are presented and discussed. Well permeability ranges from 2.36 mD to 763.00 mD and porosities between 18.44% and 28.43% respectively. The permeability of the synthetic cores was between 25.65 mD to 1389.76 mD with an average porosity of 21.81%. Reservoir samples were taken from the target areas where the CCS project is planned. The basic petrophysical properties were measured at net confining stress. Supercritical CO2 and Synthetic Brine were used. A proposed CO2 injection scheme was simulated in the laboratory to evaluate the injectivity. Relative permeability tests were performed by SteadyState method with In-Situ Saturation Monitoring (ISSM) by Linear X-ray attenuation. Parameters used in the experimental design were the initial water saturation, temperature, reservoir pressure, brine composition, and flow rate. A good injectivity associated with low pressure drop was observed in the reservoir target zones. The results obtained in this study show that during CO2 flooding, the CO2-Brine relative permeability decreases as a function of the absolute permeability. The resulting curves have different shapes and end points depending on the permeability, which indicates the importance of performing the evaluation of this property in the selected zones and not only in zones with high permeability. A map created with the end points shows the behavior of the relative permeability with brine and CO2 saturation. The saturation map can be used as a tool to select the more feasible zone for CO2 storage minimizing risks of leakage and environmental problems in long-term applications.

records.title: Accelerated Carbon Capture and Storage via Mineral Carbonation: A Laboratory-Scale Investigation
records.summary: Abstract Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) is globally recognized as a vital, strategic approach to reduce anthropogenic CO2 emissions and mitigate the adverse effects of climate change. Among various sequestration methods, mineral trapping is recognized for its superior safety and extensive CO2 storage capacity. This study presents a novel methodology for assessing the rapid mineral carbonation of CO2 through geochemical interactions with carbon-, magnesium-, and iron-rich minerals abundant in geological formations. Four minerals: olivine, dolomite, magnetite, and gypsum, have been selected as candidates for the study and exposed to CO2 at various heating rates and temperatures, utilizing Thermogravimetric Analysis/Differential Scanning Calorimetry (TGA/DSC) to establish the optimal conditions for carbon mineralization at atmospheric pressure. Furthermore, the study examined the effect of the aqueous phase with low and high ionic strength on minerals’ carbon uptake efficiency. A novel combined analysis of the minerals was conducted before and after CO2 exposure using Scanning Electron Microscopy/Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (SEM/EDS) with the normalization by TGA/DSC data to quantify the total carbon uptake by each mineral, thereby identifying the best candidate for mineral carbonation. Results showed that olivine and dolomite in a dry state displayed the highest carbon uptake values at 200˚ and 100˚ C temperatures, respectively. Thus, it was proved that accelerated carbon mineralization is possible even in the absence of an aqueous phase. However, introducing a water phase with high ionic strength to the mineral surfaces resulted in a significant increase in carbon uptake, with an average rise of 5-15 mg per 100 mg of mineral in olivine and dolomite correspondingly. Furthermore, it was found that dolomite requires more heat to store large amounts of carbon facilitated by the high heating rate of 20˚C/min, whereas olivine demonstrated higher carbon uptake values at a low heating rate of 5˚C/min. Hence, strong correlations between carbon uptake values and the heating rates for both minerals have been established. Lastly, it was concluded that the surface void spaces of the minerals were highly affected by the addition of the aqueous phase to the mineral. The pioneering approach and findings of this paper reveal that carbon storage can be successfully implemented in a matter of hours under laboratory conditions even at atmospheric pressure, effectively bridging a significant gap in the literature where experimental investigation of mineral carbonation has not been extensively explored. The results of this work provide the petroleum industry with a reliable and safe approach for accelerated CO2 sequestration in various rock formations, thus enabling the companies to successfully meet their sustainability and decarbonization objectives.

records.title: AI-Driven Optimization of Refinery Configurations: A Novel Approach to Predicting Production Outputs and Capacities
records.summary: Abstract In the context of conceptualization and operation of refineries, achieving an optimal configuration emerges as a critical endeavor. Our proposed methodology transcends conventional approaches by seamlessly integrating domain expertise, empirical insights, and cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI). Our approach holistically captures the intricate linkages between different refinery process facilities (also referred as process units or modules in later part of this paper) to make their best use in ever changing market conditions. Key aspects include robust predictive modeling for individual modules, meticulously considering feedstock availability, product demand, price information, process interdependencies and historical data. These predictions serve as foundational inputs during the conceptualization and planning stages, guiding optimal configuration decisions. Additionally, our rigorous cost modeling extends beyond capital costs to encompass financial parameters sufficient for shortlisting of configuration options for detailed economic evaluation. The machine learning models are evaluated based on the error metrices and has confirmed the models performs with in the acceptable tolerance ranges. Moreover, our integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) adeptly transforms complex refinery configurations into actionable insights expressed in business language. Decision-makers gain a holistic view, aligning technical choices with overarching organizational goals. Ultimately, this pioneering approach eases conceptualization process of new refineries and empowers operating refineries toward sustainable production and refinery-wide optimization.

records.title: AI-Driven Environmental Data Extraction for Energy Sector Assessment
records.summary: Abstract The oil and gas industry continually seeks to enhance environmental stewardship and reduce its operation carbon footprint, with carbon intensity reduction being a key objective. However, the lack of comprehensive and accessible global real operation data hinders accurate environmental assessment, climate modeling, and decision making. This challenge is exacerbated by the dispersion of crucial information across various sources and the high costs and legal aspects associated with accessing proprietary databases. This paper introduces an innovative framework leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) - specifically applying GPT-4 and GPT-4o - to extract critical oil and gas asset information from diverse literature sources. Our approach aims to bridge the gap between proprietary and open-source information, creating a more accessible database for different sectors such as industry stakeholders, policy makers, and investors. Our evaluation process rigorously assessed the LLM's performance, categorizing extractions into true positives, false positives, and false negatives. We employed key metrics including true positive rate, precision, and F1 score to balance the framework's ability to correctly identify relevant information with its capability to find all pertinent data. An iterative fine-tuning process allowed us to address specific challenges in oil and gas data extraction, such as distinguishing between active and production wells. We developed a novel LLM framework that conducts iterative comparisons between GPT-4's output and a dataset of 108 ground truth documents which were meticulously labeled by domain experts. Through 11 training and testing iterations, we fine-tuned prompts to optimize information extraction. The framework achieved impressive results, with a true positive rate of 81.44% and an F1 score of 76.78% on the testing dataset. The framework demonstrated significant efficiency gains, processing 32 documents in 61.41 minutes with GPT-4o, averaging 7.09 seconds per extraction. This represents a substantial improvement over traditional manual method. Moreover, the cost-effectiveness of the approach, with GPT-4o reducing extraction costs by a factor of 10 compared to GPT-4, makes it accessible to a wider range of researchers and organizations. This research has far-reaching implications for the oil and gas industry. By creating an organized, transparent, and accessible database, we aim to democratize access to critical information, potentially revolutionizing how data is extracted and utilized in this field and beyond. This framework could support more accurate climate modeling efforts, enhance decision-making processes for operations and investments, and contribute significantly to the sector's ability to meet environmental commitments, particularly in areas such as emissions reduction and energy transition strategies.

records.title: A Systematic Approach to Interpreting Cement Bond Logs
records.summary: Abstract To achieve a more consistent and disciplined approach, and to achieve a higher rate of accurate conclusions, a cement bond log interpretation method has been organized and applied to hundreds of operations around the world. This method approaches the bond log from a "cementing perspective" and when applied to previously interpreted logs, resulted in an accuracy increase from approximately 30 % to greater than 90 %. This study of three-hundred and twenty five wells also showed that the most common error was the misinterpretation of logs for wellbore sections containing a microannulus. This paper details a five-step process, including an example of the numerous observations and decisions that are typically made, and introduces forty-three wellbore effects that may be key to accurate bond log interpretation. Besides accuracy, the vast majority of cement bond logs have been "under-interpreted," lacking important details. This new integrated approach to bond log interpretation is designed to provide a full interpretation, hence the zonal isolation summary, the nature and cause of any cement defects, and recommendations for remediation or future improvements, are all key parts of the final interpretation.

records.title: A Sustainable Path Forward: Delivering Canada’s Longest Montney Lateral
records.summary: In pursuit of the reduction of environmental impact and increased cost effectiveness, drilling operations in the Western Canadian Sedimentary Basin (WCSB) face the unique challenge of increasing total drainage out of each surface location while reducing land impact. A major unconventional oil and gas operator and a directional drilling service provider have partnered to consistently extend lateral section lengths over 5 km and to drill the longest lateral in Canada’s Montney Play to date. The major E&P company and the service provider had delivered the first 5 successful wells with aRotary Steerable System (RSS) in 2022, having drilled the operator’s longest and fastest Montney well to date, comprised of 4734m. To consistently cross the 5km mark in the 2023 drilling campaign, both companies worked together in vibration mitigation techniques, tool ruggedness, bit selection, drillstring optimization, mud properties and utilization of vibration mitigation tools, both axial and torsional. A data-based, engineered, well-by-well strategy was customized for each of the 4 distinctive targets within the Montney formation, based on previous and current campaign findings. Through the analysis of previous 2022 drilling campaign and development of the 2023 campaign, twomain vibration mechanisms are identified as performance limiters and affecting reliability. The ability of the RSS to measure real-time High Frequency Torsional Oscillation (HFTO), one of the most damaging mechanisms in modern drilling,is utilized to reduce risk of tool damage in hard formations as the Montney. Furthermore, the analysis of high frequency vibration data is utilized to challenge the effectiveness of different types of vibration mitigation tools. The impact of mud properties in bit cutting structure,weight transfer and RSS functionality are evaluated in real time with Pressure While Drilling sensors. The article describes the use of this data to modify tool configuration, BHA, and vibration mitigation tool selection. This led to the achievement of the longest lateral section in all Canada’s Montney Play with 5287 meters, along with the longest RSS run in the Montney and the longest global run for this 4.75" RSS with 5125m. In addition to the increase in reach, performance has allowed to reduce cost per meter drilled by 12%. Ability to measure HFTO in real time increases awareness against damaging vibration within modern drilling applications. Furthermore, high-frequency 3-axial recorded vibration data allows for re-evaluation of the effects that vibration mitigation tools have in the BHA under specific circumstances. The paper confirms the feasibility of extended lateral length benchmarks in the Montney, not achievable years ago due to tool reliability impacting overall project costs. Consistently delivering laterals over 5,000m aids the sustainability of Oil&Gas development projects in culturally sensitive areas where surface location construction and access is under increased restriction.

records.title: A Study of Cement Substitution: Demonstrating Suitable Performance Helping to Reduce the CO2 Footprint
records.summary: Abstract Various environmental studies conclude the process of cement production is a significant contributor to CO2 emissions. The oilwell cementing community acknowledges the current practices may not be favorable for long term sustainability and is working towards alternative techniques as well as solutions to reduce the influence on the environment. There are various efforts underway for cement substitution or cement alternatives in an equivalent sack which emphasize mined products in the domain of geo-polymers as well as other suitable cementitious materials as opposed to the traditional methods resulting from manufacturing. A cement substitution study using an alternative cementitious material shows suitable performance when used in an equivalent sack of cement in comparison to a conventional sack of API Class G cement. The manuscript demonstrates the results of the study and how it can be used to help reduce the cement industries environmental footprint one sack at a time.

records.title: A Scalable Parallel Compositional CO2 Geological Storage Simulator
records.summary: Abstract Storing CO2 in deep saline aquifers is one of the most promising methods for achieving carbon neutrality. Numerical reservoir simulation can assist researchers and engineers in comprehensively understanding and effectively managing the CO2 sequestration process, thereby ensuring its safety and effectiveness. Most of the current CO2 storage simulators use a CO2-brine fluid model which only has water and CO2 components. When impure CO2 is injected, the subsurface fluids form a multi-component gas-brine system, whose phase behavior cannot be accurately described by a CO2-brine fluid model. The current gas-water compositional models include a very limited number of gas components. In this study, we developed a fully implicit parallel CO2 storage simulator for distributed memory computers based on our in-house parallel platform. This simulator uses a fully compositional fluid model which treats water as a component and incorporates it into phase equilibrium calculations. The gas components include not only CO2 but also other common components in captured impure CO2, such as CH4, N2 and H2S. The cubic Peng-Robinson equation of state was used to predict the fugacity and PVT properties of CO2-rich phase. The fugacity in aqueous phase and brine properties are calculated by Henry's law and empirical correlations respectively. Meanwhile, the effect of dissolved gas influence on aqueous viscosity is considered which is ignored by current commercial simulator. The finite difference (volume) method is applied to discretize the compositional fluid model. Numerical experiments show that our simulator is scalable, stable and validated to simulate large-scale CO2 storage problems with hundreds of millions of grid blocks on a parallel supercomputer cluster.

records.title: A Producer-Based Capacitance Resistance Model (CRM) to Characterize Oil Reservoirs with Natural Water Influx: a Realistic Application
records.summary: Abstract In water-drive reservoirs, predicting variable water influx to individual wells poses significant challenges due to geological heterogeneity and diverse production strategies. This study introduces a novel capacitance-resistance model (CRM) that robustly incorporates natural water influx into oil reservoirs from aquifer systems, eliminating the need for average reservoir and aquifer pressure versus time data. The proposed aquifer-integrated CRM addresses the pressure change equation between the aquifer and reservoir systems using fundamental CRM parameters including aquifer pore volume and productivity index. The development process focuses on the CRM with producer representation (CRMP) and reformulates it to calculate instantaneous water influx based on reservoir and aquifer pressure differences, naming this model CRMPAQ. The history matching algorithm utilizes Sequential Least-Squares Programming (SLSQP) to manage both inequality and equality constraints, employing linear inequality constraints to ensure that the summation of aquifer-producer connectivity and well-to-well connectivity does not exceed unity. Additionally, a linear equality constraint ensures that the summation of producer pore volumes equals the total reservoir pore volume. The CRMPAQ model is designed to match total production rates and bottomhole pressures (BHPs), if available. Numerical experiments conducted using CRMPAQ on both 3D synthetic and realistic field datasets demonstrate its effectiveness. Comparisons with results from the commercial simulator ECLIPSE, which accounts for saturation dependency on well productivity, further validate the model. The realistic field dataset comprises three wells from a heterogeneous reservoir with natural water influx, frequent shut-ins, and variable skin effects, with daily records of production rates and BHPs. The results indicate that CRMPAQ yields comparable outcomes and effectively emulates the behavior of high-fidelity reservoir simulators in terms of total liquid production rates and BHP data. CRMPAQ is significantly more computationally efficient; two to three orders of magnitude faster than high-fidelity simulator history matching. Furthermore, when matching BHP data using flow rate history, CRMPAQ accurately accounts for the effects of frequent shut-ins as well as the variable productivity indices on parameter estimation. The model was tested on synthetic datasets and validated with a realistic field dataset (used in SPE-210102-PA). The realistic dataset considers three wells produced from a heterogeneous reservoir with natural water influx, frequent shut-ins, and variable skin effects. The wells' production rates and BHP data are recorded at daily time intervals.

records.title: A Practical Framework for CO2 Transportation and Injection Design by Analyzing Both Technical and Economic Aspects
records.summary: Abstract The main objective of this research is to propose a practical framework for CO2 transportation and injection design by analyzing the impact of pipeline length and mass flowrate on cost-effective aspects. Numerical methods are applied using experimental data of CO2 properties at different pressures and temperatures to provide the most accurate model designs for CO2 transporting and injection considering both technical and economic aspects. This paper used an open-source coding language to integrate the physical and thermodynamic properties of CO2 into software to predict phase behavior, viscosity, density, entropy, etc. under different pressure and temperature conditions. This simulator was then expanded using advanced hydraulic models to predict static and dynamic behaviors of CO2 in pipelines and tubing with and without booster pumps. Sensitivity analysis was carried out to study the effects of pipeline length, mass flowrate, and the number of booster pumps on the economic aspect of CO2 transportation and storage. A case study was performed using the developed computational model to optimize a hypothetical CO2 transportation system in the Permian Basin to minimize the CO2 project's cost. The obtained results showed that using the developed computational simulator for designing CO2 transportation and injection provides more reliable prediction for pressure and temperature profiles without using correlations for CO2 properties. The sensitivity analysis reveals that the number of booster pumps and pipe diameter are the two key variables in designing a CO2 transportation and storage system. The next sensitive variables are the mass injection rate and the pipe length. The results from the case study showed that there is no universal design solution when it comes to CO2 transportation and storage design; instead, each project must be tuned and optimized accordingly by varying all the inputs. The developed software can help optimize CO2 transportation based on a specific desired system with a specific desired injection rate.

records.title: A Permian Microgrid Case Study - Keys to Successful Implementations
records.summary: Abstract As the oil and gas industry's interest in more electrified solutions continues to grow, the demand for more complex power management systems is on the rise. While utilizing utility power to energize a wellsite can help lower emissions, the utility's power typically isn't sufficient to meet a wellsite's high-power demands. Additionally, some applications have very aggressive loads which can conflict with utility companies' aims to keep power steady 24/7. Given these dynamics, understanding the different options available when selecting a power source for a wellsite is imperative to maximize the benefit of all available resources without impacting operations. This paper examines key considerations for successfully erecting a microgrid system in the oilfield that includes a variety of distributed energy resources (DER) such as gensets and energy storage systems interconnected to a power grid, as well as the option of not only importing power from the grid but also exporting power if needed. Approaches to customize a microgrid to fulfill a wellsite's unique requirements will also be highlighted. A case study of a wellsite in the Permian powered by a microgrid will be shared. This example will explain how the wellsite, which can require up to 25 megawatts (MW) of power, can successfully operate on 10 MW from the utility with 15 MW supplemented by gas-fueled gensets. It will also cover how the power management system allowed the operator to reduce the need for on-site power generation by 40% by replacing that power demand with grid power.

records.title: A Novel Solid Lubricant Designed Using Tribology Science Reduces the Torque and Improve ROP in Water Base Mud Wells in the Llanos Basin and Magdalena Valley of Colombia
records.summary: Abstract An Operator in Colombia was experiencing torque issues in a water-based fluid system while drilling wells in the Middle Magdalena and Llanos basins. To address these torque issues, a novel solid lubricant was presented to the operator by the fluid service provider and product manufacturer. Through an extensive lab testing profile, utilizing traditional testing protocols in addition to introducing tribology, the lubricant was selected for field trials. Further testing of the field samples was completed, and data collected from the wellsite demonstrated torque reduction and increased rate of penetration (ROP) allowing the operator to complete the interval. Tribology uses a different approach to explain stick-slip phenomena and variations of torque and drag. Tribometer results are plotted on a Stribeck curve to display the coefficient of friction as a non-linear function of the contact load. This shows the continuous variations in the different lubrication regimes. The coefficient of friction (COF), static, is due to the contact between bottom hole assembly (BHA) and wellbore is recurrent while drilling directional wellbores. Tribometer results demonstrated the solid lubricant adhered to the disk asperities, reducing the difference between static and dynamic coefficients of friction. This reduction was confirmed during the field trial and additionally the ROP was increased after the addition of the lubricant. Use of a single value COF to build torque and drag modeling produces an oversimplified representation of a lubricant’s COF improvement. When instead using a tribometer to create a Stribeck curve a lab’s results produce applicable data, as it incorporates variations of rotation and load. More attention should be dedicated to the performance of lubricants in the boundary condition in directional wells as this represents the torque required to initiate rotation and overcome differential pressure while making connections. Use of the novel lubricant reduces static COF and breakover torque. Tribology, the science of friction, lubrication and wear has been used in automotive, space, pharmaceutical and mechanical engineering industries among others for years for the design and evaluation of solid and liquid lubricants. Unfortunately, this is not a common practice in the oil and gas industry. Tribology allows better understanding of wellbore lubrication throughout the different regimes and under differing loads. Tribology is a new method to measure the complex phenomena of lubricity in the oilfield. It helps better understand items such as stick-slip and torque variations while drilling and how they can be explained through analyzing their behavior along the Stribeck curve.

records.title: A Novel Approach for Gas Delivery Optimization of a Complex Pipeline Network System Using Hybrid Physics–Machine Learning Modeling
records.summary: Abstract Traditionally, physics-driven simulation models have primarily been employed for design and long-term forecasting purposes. However, maintaining the accuracy of the model's boundary conditions and achieving convergence for operational decisions have posed significant challenges. Consequently, operators do not commonly use these physics-based models for optimizing daily operations, relying instead on personal judgment and experience. In this work, we introduce a novel and agile approach for optimizing gas delivery using hybrid physics–machine learning (ML) modeling. It is applied in a complex onshore pipeline system connected to multiple midstream sales points. Given the fluctuating gas prices and daily operational constraints with the need to meet the daily production quotas, there is a significant demand for a robust, agile optimization solution. This solution must manage day-to-day decision-making processes, considering the ever-changing field and market conditions. The system in this project comprises 80 pads and four delivery sites, each with its unique set of flow and pressure constraints. These include minimum and maximum flow rates at delivery points and a cap on the maximum allowable pressure within the network. The flow into delivery points is regulated through per-site choke adjustments, adding another layer of complexity to the optimization process. The core objective of the proposed solution is to maximize total revenue. This is achieved by optimizing gas production across the four delivery sites while adhering to all flow and pressure constraints. This balance is crucial for operational efficiency and profitability. The solution is built on a novel hybrid of physics-ML models, employing surrogate modeling techniques. This approach combines the accuracy of physics-based models with the efficiency and adaptability of ML. The model is trained on thousands of scenarios generated from high-fidelity physics-based flow simulations. These simulations incorporate detailed aspects of multiphase flow, pressure losses, heat transfer, and rigorous pressure-volume-temperature analysis. Additionally, the model's flexible application programming interface facilitates integration across various platforms, enhancing its applicability. The hybrid ML model demonstrates remarkable efficiency, capable of solving complex scenarios in mere seconds. This efficiency translates into approximately 2,000 solves per optimization, completed within 2 to 10 seconds—a stark contrast to the 33 hours required by a flow simulator. Despite its incredible speed, the surrogate model's predictions have an impressive accuracy rate of 99% against physics-based models. This solution marks a significant transformation from traditional methods, which heavily relied on personal judgment and experience. By integrating data-driven insights integrated with the detailed physics of multiphase flow and gas production, the proposed approach allows for rapid, informed decision making. This maximizes our gas production revenues and ensures the integrity of our pipelines.

records.title: A New Simplified Kinetic Model for Hydrogen Generation During In-Situ Combustion Gasification of Heavy Oil
records.summary: Abstract In the global push for sustainable energy, in-situ combustion gasification (ISCG) has emerged as a transformative technology to leverage the world's abundant heavy oil reserves for producing carbon-zero hydrogen. Chemical kinetics are crucial for modeling subsurface hydrogen generation and optimizing production schemes to maximize hydrogen yield, which are however currently lacking. This study aims to develop the first experimentally validated kinetic model for hydrogen generation during ISCG of heavy oil. To accurately model ISCG reactions, particularly hydrogen generation, we combined kinetic cell experiments with numerical modeling to history-match the experimental results. The temporal variation of generated gases, such as hydrogen, measured in laboratory experiments, served as the baseline for history matching. A differential evolution optimization algorithm was employed to calibrate the kinetic parameters of the numerical model with experimental results. The kinetic model for combustion reactions was accurately calibrated using combustion experiments. This accuracy is attributed to the well-studied nature of heavy oil oxidation and the comprehensive reaction scheme employed. Conversely, calibrating the kinetic model for gasification reactions with kinetic cell experimental results proved more challenging. Despite significant uncertainties in hydrogen generation and consumption reactions due to limited knowledge of the gasification process, our proposed kinetic model can still predict hydrogen generation with a simplified but powerful reaction scheme, compared to previously proposed ISCG models that involve numerous reactions. This work introduces the first kinetic model to describe the hydrogen generation process during ISCG of heavy oil with rigorous experimental validation. This reliable kinetic model establishes a solid foundation for future multi-scale reservoir simulation and further optimization of the field development for enhanced hydrogen production in a more sustainable manner.

records.title: A New Approach Towards Flow Diagnostic in High-Rate Gas Wells
records.summary: Abstract High gas rate wells flowing up to 80 MMscfd pose challenges for flow diagnostics. Conventional methods for measuring gas and water holdups, such as local electrical probes, fail in these extreme conditions due to the extremely small droplets and hydrodynamic effects. Approaches based on fluid column density measurements suffer from large inaccuracies due to friction effects. The paper describes the sensor technology and field results from a high gas rate well with small water cut and complex flow regime. To overcome these challenges, an operating company worked with a service and manufacturing company to improve a compact toolstring capable of delivering reliable flow data (holdups and phase velocity) for phase allocation over an interval with multiple zones and different fluid properties. The toolstring developed is shorter than conventional tools (just over three foot long) and causes minimal flow disturbance. Azimuthal phase holdups and velocities are collocated with one foot away auxiliary measurements of pressure, temperature, MEMS Magnetic Locator (MML) for casing collar detection and depth correlation, tool orientation, and deviation. The flow array sensors consist of triphasic optical probes, conductivity probes, micro-capacitances, Doppler, and wide-range robust micro-spinners. Segregated flow with water recirculation was observed. The micro-capacitances provided the most reliable source for water holdup while the electrical probes in mist flow, as expected, stopped detecting water at flow speeds of 2 m/s. The triphasic optical probes showed good gas hold up measurements at the whole range of flow velocities in the well and responded to a small water entry in the middle of the perforated zone. All micro-spinners rotated well throughout the survey even at the highest rate. The radar sonde detected water droplets down to micrometer size using the retro diffusion of light electromagnetic signal at a distance from the sensor surface. While the EM radar senses water movement inside the mist flow, the Doppler sensors allowed to monitor movement in the water dominant leg at the well bottom. Thanks to integrating all types of sensors physics, a robust flow diagnostic allowed the operator to understand the water and gas entries, while the conventional sensors could not, and consider remedial actions for water shutoff. The present sensor configuration and tool string can be used as reference for logging in the same field or similar flow conditions. In order to detect water, two novel sensors were developed: micro-capacitance probes to measure water holdup and electromagnetic radar for measuring flow speed. The standalone radar module operates in high velocity flow and does not require direct contact between droplets and the sensing element, as micrometer size water droplets can be detected with the retro diffusion of light EM signal at a distance from the sensor surface.

records.title: A New Algorithm for Automated ISIP Interpretation
records.summary: Abstract In multi-stage unconventional horizontal wells instantaneous shut-in pressure (ISIP) is useful for the analysis of hydraulic fracturing and its interaction with the stress state in the reservoir. ISIP can be estimated from the leak-off pressure response after the end of the treatment. However, this value is normally eclipsed by pressure oscillations that occur immediately after well shut-in, known as water hammer, which complicate its interpretation. We developed an automated workflow to estimate ISIP values from fracture stages that allows for the utilization of various shut-in physical models. The workflow is based on guidelines proposed by Roussel et al. (2021) and incorporates the Trust Region Reflective algorithm to optimize all parameters in the model, which allows for model convergence in a wider range of cases and is validated using field data. Comparison of fitting model parameters between stages and the addition of a ‘goodness of fit’ metric allow for quick identification of outliers and poorly matched model predictions. ISIP estimations at different step-down rate managements were then compared for validation using a commercial hydraulic fracture simulator capable of reproducing water hammer. Simulations showed that ISIP interpretation is consistent at varying step-down rates. Additionally, water hammer frequency in each stage of the well was converted into depth to test its potential as a diagnostic tool for fracture stage isolation by comparing results to observations made through fiber optic measurements.

records.title: A New Acid for Extending the Lifetime of Wireline Cables with Spearhead Applications
records.summary: Abstract Acid spearheading is a known practice in both vertical and horizontal hydraulic fracturing operations. The practice became very common during horizontal well completion aiming at dissolving acid-soluble material in the near-wellbore area, cleaning perforation tunnels, lowering the initiation breakdown pressure, and enhancing injectivity. Low- to mid-strength hydrochloric acid with additives is the commonly applied fluid. However, acid incompatibility with perforating guns and wireline tools mandates separating the perforation creation and tunnel cleaning stages, resulting in longer completion time and additional wellbore fluid to be used. Although "compatible" acids have been recently introduced to perforate-in-acid, their ability to effectively protect wireline cables is questionable. The repetitive use of the wireline leads to significant corrosion, which significantly impacts the cable integrity to the point of mechanical failure. Wireline cable armors are galvanized (zinc-coated) plow steel, which is particularly challenging to protect against corrosion. The zinc layer is approximated at 4 to 5 wt% of the wire armor. A new acid utilizing a specially designed corrosion inhibitor (CI-A) was able to provide an excellent protection to zinc and maintain the protective layer. As a result, less maintenance and substantial increase in the lifetime of the wireline cable are anticipated. The effectiveness of the new acid was investigated in corrosion testing on pure zinc coupons and wireline armors and compared to a benchmark standard industry "modified" acid (BMSA) at a temperature up to 190°F. Testing duration varied from 2 to 24 hours and optimum load was determined for two HCl concentrations: 5 and 7.5 wt%. Mechanical integrity of the cables was assessed through ductility "wrapping" testing after exposure to the acid under test. Two types of wireline cables were tested, conventional and jacketed cables. Corrosion testing on L-80 and P-110 tubular materials was also conducted. Microscopic imaging was utilized to better visualize the deposited layer on the wireline surface. The new acid utilizing corrosion inhibitor CI-A showed rapid and excellent deposition on the zinc surface resulting in a weight loss between 0 and 0.5% based on the testing duration, temperature, and acid concentration. Repetitive exposure of the same wire to the inhibited acid showed a negative weight loss indicating excellent deposition and longer lifetime expectations. On the other hand, the BMSA acid failed with 5 to 7% weight loss indicating a complete loss to the protective zinc layer and significant corrosion to the steel beneath it. Wire armors exposed to acid inhibited by CI-A passed all ductility testing successfully. Armors exposed to the BMSA acid broke within the first wrapping cycle. Both acids provided an adequate protection to casing metals, which cannot be the sole criterion for a compatible spearhead acid during perforation. The new acid with the proposed corrosion inhibitor allows using hydrochloric acid with wireline cables without the risk of corrosion or impacting the wireline mechanical integrity, resulting in a longer lifetime. Moreover, with perforating-in-acid, additional time is saved per stage, wellbore fluid volume is reduced, and pumping time and, hence, emissions are reduced.

records.title: A Low Cost Microproppant for Flattening Production Declines Using an Industrial Byproduct
records.summary: Abstract Unconventional reservoir production declines are notoriously steep in part due to up to 75% to 90% of the flow area being unpropped (Barba 2015 and Sharma 2015.) The second referenced study coined the term "induced unpropped" (IU) fractures to describe the flow path in the unpropped portions of the reservoir. As the closure stress on the reservoir increases with depletion these are more likely to close off than propped fractures and can result in a gradual reduction in total flow area. In addition to the steep declines there are two other indications that many of these IU fractures do not remain conductive as the effective stress increases. The first is that the production "bump" from an offset well FDI typically returns the to the original decline in approximately two to three years (Gupta 2012). A possible mechanism is the offset well was stimulated with the distal extent of a low or unpropped conductivity fracture that degraded with the effective stress increase from depletion. A second indication is the reduction in producing height in time lapse geochemical surveys (Ge 2022). With the low viscosity fluids, fracture widths are already challenged especially at as the distance from the lateral to the IU fractures increases with increasingly less hydraulic pressure due to friction losses. Natural fractures and induced microfractures have been shown to have aperture widths of generally less than 0.1 mm (Anders 2014). In theory, if these sub 100 mesh width (less than 0.15 mm) IU fractures can be propped with microproppant during the treatment to maintain conductivity flow can possibly be maintained. The P50 mesh size for fly ash is 320 mesh with a range from 800 to 200. There have been multiple studies done that show this can happen even with relatively small microproppant volumes and suggests this theory has credence. In spite of these largely positive results the use of microproppant has not been widely adopted in organic shale completions. In the case of one major operator that did several trials and published positive results they have cut back their microproppant use due to the high cost of the currently commercially available products. This study proposes that a significantly lower cost system is available with fly ash. Fly ash is an industrial byproduct from coal fired power plants. The P50 size is 320 mesh and has a similar mesh size distribution to the current commercially available ceramic products. It has been shown to create high conductivity fracture systems in over 70 wells as a stand-alone proppant. The delivered cost is approximately the same as Ottowa which is approximately half of the cost of the commercial ceramic products. With the higher cost commercially available microproppants operators typically pump relatively small volumes. The operator mentioned earlier that had seen success with microproppants in the Bakken had been pumping a maximum of 2% of the stage proppant volumes due to the high cost per pound. With the use of fly ash the microproppant cost per pound will not increase for operators already pumping Ottowa (as in the Bakken) and will only increase by a factor of plus or minus two for local sand treatments vs a factor of four for the ceramic products already on the market.

records.title: A Hybrid Tabular-Spatial-Temporal Model with 3D Geo-Model for Production Prediction in Shale Gas Formations
records.summary: Abstract The evolution of shale gas production has reshaped North America's energy profile. Utilizing the vast amounts of data generated from production and operations, machine learning offers significant advantages in production forecasting and performance optimization. This study proposed a pioneering hybrid model integrating tabular, spatial, and temporal modalities to enhance production forecasting in unconventional shale gas reservoirs. Despite traditional methods such as artificial neural networks (ANN) and XGBoost, which rely solely on tabular data for training and prediction, this study proposes a novel 3D-parameterization method. This approach tokenizes the formation property distribution into 3-axis tensors, enabling a more comprehensive representation of spatial data. Then, a 3D-convolutional neural network (3D-CNN) with the attention mechanism module was established to process the created spatial data. For temporal modality, the long short-term memory (LSTM) module was used to accept the dynamic input and predict the monthly production simultaneously. A total of 677 wells data from Duvernay formation was collected, pre-processed and fed into the according module based on their modality. The results show that the model combined three modalities achieved an impressive level of accuracy, with a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.8771, surpassing the tabular (0.7841) and tabular-spatial (0.8230) modalities models. Additionally, global optimization was applied to further enhance the model performance by optimizing the architecture of each module and model hyperparameters, and a 1.88% improvement was achieved from the empirical design. These advancements set a new benchmark for predictive modelling in unconventional shale gas reservoirs, highlighting the importance of utilizing data from different modalities in improving production forecast prediction.

records.title: A Hybrid Approach for Production Forecasting and Uncertainty Characterization
records.summary: Abstract RGNet (Reservoir Graph Network) is a pragmatic reduced-physics model that utilizes the essential physics of flow in porous media while simplifying computational complexities. Its versatility has been demonstrated through successful applications in a range of reservoir management applications, including reservoir connectivity analysis, resource volume estimation, dynamic forecasting, well control optimization, flood optimization, and integration with surface network models. While RGNet has been proven effective, there is a vision for further enhancing its modeling precision and predictive capabilities by incorporating advanced machine learning (ML) techniques. In this study, we propose a hybrid approach which combines RGNet and ML for production forecasting with uncertainty characterization. The basic idea is to use RGNet-simulated data as training features and use sparse regression (SpR) to select the important features and fit a data-driven model between the features and the target output. To forecast into the future, we substitute the simulated data of the future period into the SpR model to obtain the corresponding forecasted target output. For training purposes, we only need a rough prior model to start with and the calibrated model is not required, which significantly reduces the manual effort in history matching. In addition, as the training and prediction are very fast to perform, the same procedure can be repeated for multiple prior realizations in quite short time, which enables the uncertainty characterization of the future performance. The proposed hybrid RGNet-SpR method was tested on a deep-water field case to see whether it can improve the forecast performance of BHP. For training purposes, multiple prior RGNet realizations are randomly generated and simulated to generate the training features. The features considered relevant include simulated well-level injection/production rates and BHP data. As the simulation system are controlled using gas/water injection rates for gas/water injectors and using oil production rates for oil producers, these control variables as input features are also the historical production data in the training process. The output targets are BHP of target wells, which include multiple wells. As RGNet-SpR fits coefficients for different features, we use the magnitude of the features to characterize the strength of the connectivity between the target well and feature well. The proposed workflow is quite robust even when we use less than 50% of available data for training to obtain good quality forecasts. Also, multiple forecasts are shown to span the unseen data with a relatively small error band. Combining RGNet with ML provides a more robust and efficient solution for production forecasting with capability for uncertainty characterization. The proposed solution does not require a history-matched model as the base model, which saves resources and enables faster decision making.

records.title: A Field Application of Machine Learning for Sonic Log Prediction and In-Situ Stress Estimation in Natural Buttes, Uinta Basin, Utah
records.summary: Abstract It is necessary to use sonic logs in gathering rock mechanical properties which are used to estimate in-situ stresses which are useful for fracture design and reservoir characterization. However, the high cost of its acquisition deters companies from getting complete well measurements and in some cases, we may have incomplete sonic log data due to tool damage, poor calibration, and other reasons. In other cases, the well of interest might only have a triple combo suite to determine target depths and left up to engineering judgment what a hydraulic fracture might look like. This study shows a field application of machine learning (ML) algorithms using triple combo logs to predict elastic properties and finally estimate in-situ stress profile in the Natural Buttes gas field. We used a complete set of triple combo and dipole sonic logs to train K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) regression and Bi-directional convolutional long short-term memory (Bi-ConvLSTM) models. A data preparation and transformation technique were applied to reduce heteroscedasticity by manipulating data distribution. Then, prediction-performances were compared to each other, and a selected ML model went through a validation to verify it effectively captures existing patterns in the well log data. The selected ML model was finally deployed into a GUI interface which is helpful for users to create predictions, visualize and analyze the generated results. Comparative analysis of ML models shows that the KNN mitigates overprediction observed in the Bi-ConvLSTM. The KNN reduces training time while the Bi-ConvLSTM is computationally expensive as it considers well log data as an image. We also quantify uncertainty of KNN predictions through a heuristic approach to provide uncertainty thresholds as decision boundary for in-situ stress estimation. For calibration verification, we present one data set showing the predicted sonic velocities vs actual measured velocities as well as the predicted vs actual elastic and in-situ stress profile. The GUI can deploy trained models, take test data for prediction, visualize triple combo logs, predicted sonic logs, calculated elastic properties and in-situ stresses with variances for analysis. We conducted fracture modeling using a commercial numerical simulation tool for both the measured and synthetic cases and found the SRV was similar to each other. This study demonstrates that the use of machine learning combined with well-established data transformation, uncertainty estimation, and visualization can reduce time and cost in extracting and analyzing a valuable information. Based on literature review, this is the first time that such a workflow has been shown up to the in-situ stresses portion of the workflow. We finally, perform hydraulic fracture simulation on the synthetic in-situ stress profile case and show equivalent results to the calibrated in-situ stress profile case.

records.title: A Digital Rock Physics Approach to Modeling Permeability Changes with Solid Phase Formation in Reservoir Porous Media
records.summary: Abstract This paper illustrates the application of pore-scale numerical simulation to evaluate permeability changes due to solids precipitation with Digital Rock Physics (DRP). A DRP modeling workflow is used to quantify permeability changes due to solid phase formation (precipitation of gas hydrates) based on their deposition morphology on the pore scale. Virtual representations of a sandstone sample from the Bentheimer outcrop are created using micro-computer-tomography (micro-CT) scanning images and state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms. The binarized images (pores and grains) are systematically altered with morphological operations, i.e., erosion and dilation, to represent precipitation of solids in a pore filling and a grain/pore coating morphology, respectively. The Lattice Boltzmann Method (LBM) for single-phase fluid flow simulations is used to calculate the absolute permeability of the original and the altered 3D rock models directly on the pore structure. The changes of permeability are plotted against the solid saturation to compare to empirically derived and idealistic, mathematical descriptions. We verify the suitability of the high-resolution micro-CT images for fluid flow simulations using guidelines from the technical literature. Due to the high permeability and porosity of the sample, a threshold algorithm for image binarization based on the Otsu criterion is used and yields a sample porosity of 0.28 and permeability of 4.77 Darcy in z-direction. These values for porosity and permeability are validated from measurements using a CMS-300 apparatus on the actual rock sample. Erosion is applied to the segmented pore space to represent the pore filling deposition morphology and dilation is applied to the segmented grains to represent the grain/pore coating deposition morphology of methane hydrates. A third-degree polynomial trend relating the permeability reduction with the hydrate saturation is established for the first time using the actual pore structure rather than idealized and empirically derived laws, which are non-unique, depending on which theoretical method is chosen. The presented methodology could be used to evaluate the effect of solids precipitation on scenarios like the productivity of petroleum reservoirs, and injectivity in carbon sequestration or gas storage projects.

records.title: A Cost-Effective Pump-Down Falloff Pressure Test for Pore Pressure and Closure Pressure Evaluation
records.summary: Abstract High resolution surface pressure data is increasingly being acquired not only during the hydraulic fracture treatment, but also during and after the wireline pump-down and perforating phases. While pump-down falloff pressure data recently became more accessible, it has not commonly been analyzed as a Diagnostic Fracture Injection Test (DFIT) because the pump-down procedure doesn't follow standard DFIT practices. It is common that after perforating the first stage, pump-down operation is immediately followed by a hydraulic fracture treatment to increase operating efficiency. The immediacy of this practice forfeits an opportunity to collect important post-perforation falloff pressure data which may be analyzed to understand rock properties. This paper introduces a cost-effective procedure to evaluate pore pressure and closure pressure by introducing small changes to pump-down practices. The method begins with a wireline pump-down at 2-15 bpm to the toe of the lateral, then continues with an injection usually at 2 bpm while perforating the first stage, concluding with an extended shut-in. The operator perforates the toe stage with a wet casing shoe at least 7 to 10 days before frac fleet arrival to ensure there is no issue pumping into the well for the first stage. Duration of the extended shut-in (falloff) and volume of water pumped while perforating do not significantly differ from the duration and injected volume for a DFIT. But, unlike DFITs where a pump truck is mobilized to location after the toe prep is completed, the pump-down falloff test is performed as an integral part of the pump-down operations, therefore eliminating the need to dispatch pumping personnel and equipment to perform a separate DFIT pump-down. The test can be done during the first stage perforating operation of plug-and-perf completed horizontal wells using real-time high-resolution pressure gauges that record pump-down injection rates and pressures. The operator has successfully performed the extended pump-down falloff pressure tests in 12 horizontal wells in the Williston Basin. The results of these tests were validated with offset DFITs. The closure and pore pressure results from both methods were in good agreement, but with some depletion observed in the most recent wells drilled. This paper shows that not only can we estimate pore pressure (p¯), but also closure pressure for the "total rock system" affected by the injection using the first stage's pump-down and perforating falloff pressure data without conducting a conventional DFIT. The authors also analyzed pump-down pressure decline data for all other stages to identify stages with reservoir pressure depletion or potential communications with offset fracs or prior stages (stress shadow) along the lateral allowing the frac design to be adjusted if needed prior to pumping the stages (e.g., pump a smaller treatment when a stage is depleted). The proposed pump-down falloff tests are operationally practical and may be used as an alternative option in evaluating pore pressure and closure pressure differences among wells on multi-well pads.

records.title: A Comprehensive Feasibility Study of a Production Technique to Lift Extra-Heavy, High-Viscosity Oil with an ESP System Demonstrates Improvement of Flow Assurance and Oil Production
records.summary: Abstract An Ecuadorian oil company recorded multiple early failures of electric submersible pumps (ESP) due to harsh fluid conditions. The extra-heavy (9°API) and high-viscosity (10,000) oil at surface stopped production from a new promising reservoir with approximately 400 million barrels of oil reserves. An oil service company studied the feasibility of injecting hot water in the wellbore to lift the viscous fluid using an ESP by reducing oil's viscosity and improving flow assurance conditions from downhole to surface. The studied production technique injects field-produced hot water in the wellbore through a dual concentric tubing string, controlling injection flow rate and pressure with self-regulated downhole valves, to prevent pressure interference with the reservoir's productivity. The hot water heats the oil, reducing fluid viscosity through the ESP and the tubing. A comprehensive technical feasibility study was carried out by a multidisciplinary team of domain experts using a transient-state, multiphase fluid flow simulator to integrate reservoir performance, fluid dynamics, completion architecture, and ESP operation into one holistic, robust model to analyze various production and sensibility scenarios over time in a selected well candidate. The holistic study demonstrated the proposed production technique could be a cost-effective, technically feasible solution to resume production from the promising reservoir that contained the extra-heavy, high-viscosity oil. On the ESP system side, there was a substantial increase of pump efficiency by 7 times, while the motor's working temperature was reduced by 12%, two factors that would help to extend ESPs run life. For the fluid, the simulation of the production technique proved how injecting hot water would improve fluid mobility, showing a reduction of surface fluid viscosity from 10,000 cP to 1,000 cP, while downhole viscosity dropped from 900 cP to 240 cP; thus, the friction losses in the tubing string declined by 89%. Such improvement in flow assurance conditions and ESP efficiency had one main benefit compared to a conventional ESP configuration producing the extra-heavy oil in the same well candidate: optimization of oil flow rate by 20%. Furthermore, economics of the well improved by the extension of ESP run life expectancy, avoiding workovers, and optimizing flow rate. The innovative production technique represented a more cost-effective solution than a conventional ESP installation by 5.4 times This technique emerges as a solution to meet the challenges presented by the extra-heavy, high-viscosity oil in the studied reservoir; it could allow the operator to reactivate production in 15 wells, where other implemented production configurations have failed to avoid early ESP failures caused by flow assurance problems. The study of the proposed method proved it is technically feasible and is more cost-effective than a conventional ESP configuration.

records.title: A Comparative Analysis of Completion and Reservoir Data to Decipher Productivity Drivers in North American Tight and Shale Plays
records.summary: Abstract The primary objective of this study is to thoroughly assess the influence of various completion, fracturing stimulation, and intrinsic reservoir properties affecting productivity of ten major unconventional oil and gas plays while uncovering key insights and emerging trends unique to each play. We examined a dataset comprising of 91,519 horizontal wells that began production on or after January 1st, 2015, across ten major unconventional oil and gas plays (Bakken, Delaware, Duvernay, Midland, Eagle Ford, Scoop|Stack, Haynesville, Marcellus, Montney, and Utica) in North America. The analysis centered on four main aspects: well fracturing, downhole consumables, production, and geological properties. The horizontal and vertical well spacings were based on the horizontal and vertical distance between the target wellbore and its closest near neighbor in any zone, respectively. The wells were classified as parent, child, or co-completed based on the distance and timeframe between their completion. The Bakken-US play shows the most remarkable increase in normalized production per 1000 ft of lateral, almost doubling from 2015 to 2024, while Scoop|Stack experienced a decline in normalized production. Bakken and Montney, with high TOC, had low normalized productivity, whereas Utica, despite low TOC, was highly productive, underscoring completion quality's importance over organic quality. Although high brittleness is usually seen as beneficial for promoting fracturing, it is intriguing to note that plays with fewer wells per pad (e.g., Scoop|Stack) exhibit a higher growth rate of fractures, even when they have a lower brittleness index (median < 0.34). Horizontal spacing plays a crucial role in optimizing performance. Less productive plays benefit from denser development. Co-completed wells outperform other sequencing, indicating their ability to mitigate "frac hits" or fracture-driven interactions. Longer laterals offer better resource contact, but productivity does not increase linearly. Sand remained the predominant proppant used in all plays due to cost-effectiveness. Freshwater remains the dominant frac fluid across all plays, and slickwater frac jobs consistently yield high productivity. The type of chemicals in terms of their dominant use varies across plays, but the trend in each play is largely unchanged since 2015. The number of clusters per stage varies across plays, and increasing the number of clusters may not always lead to enhanced productivity due to the stress shadowing effect. This study offers important insights into factors affecting productivity in shale plays, aiding future well development and resource extraction optimization. It provides technical guidance for unconventional oil and gas developments in North America and is a useful reference for similar projects globally, including in China.

records.title: 60 Years of UUU Fields – Leveraging on Big Industry Technology Applications for Rejuvenating the Foremost Niger Delta Condensate Gas-Development Asset
records.summary: Abstract The UUU cluster is the largest condensate gas producing (peak rate - 400 MMscf/d) asset in onshore Western Niger Delta. It comprises UghE, UghW and UtoR (UUU) dual hydrocarbon production fields which were discovered in 1959, 1960 and 1964 respectively. In the last decade, field redevelopment campaign which was premised on extensive integrated sub-surface studies was initiated to rejuvenate the asset and increase production target to 0.5 Bscf/day. Gas condensate is contained in high-permeability (150 – 1,000 md) sandstone reservoirs between 8,000 and 15,000 ft subsea depth. There are a total of 14 producing gas wells with 15 producing intervals (including one dual string, dual completion). Three gas processing plants with nominal capacities of 360 MMscf/d, 150 MMscf/d and 90 MMscf/d are utilised to process the produced wet gas prior to export for domestic and West African consumption. The proximity of the producing gas fields created an excellent opportunity for integrated production operations management, surface facilities sharing and cost optimisation. In the aftermath of the 2012 western asset ownership transfer from Shell Nigeria, attention was focused on maintaining optimal production targets through the following activities: Execution of in-fill development opportunities within the cluster Recovery of production from matured "locked-in" reserves Production facilities revamp and integrity management Deployment of cost-effective processes and new technology applications for CAPEX and OPEX reduction The asset management activities included successful deployment of seismic data reprocessing and interpretation, new well drilling and workovers, integrated asset modelling and management processes, flow assurance and well integrity management activities, surface facilities debottlenecking, advanced data acquisition campaign including multi-phase flow metering, and other low-cost, well intervention retrofit applications. All these efforts have resulted in sustained natural gas production of over 300 MMscf/d with associated 5,000 bpd of condensate in the past decade. This paper describes how UUU fields condensate gas development and production performance has evolved over the past 60 years; the well, reservoir and facility management challenges encountered along with the big industry technology applications adopted for sustained production. It is expected that this paper will shed light on those elements that are critical to sustaining production in analogue brown fields.

records.title: 3D Integrated Fracture-Hit Mitigation and Fracture Complexity Enhancement Technology for Deep Shale: A Successful Story in the Southern Sichuan Basin
records.summary: Abstract With continuous development of mid-shallow shale gas reservoirs, the focus gradually shifts to deep shale reservoirs (depth>3500 m) that contribute to over 65% of total shale gas resources in the Southern Sichuan Basin. In this area, large-scale and high-intensity fracturing (pumping rate: >20 m3/min; sand loading intensity: 2-3.1 t/m) is the commonly used stimulation approach to achieve larger stimulated reservoir volume (SRV). However, the complex tectonic evolution generates well-developed and large-scale natural fractures/faults which can penetrate several horizontal wells and offer high risk of fracture hits, impairing well productivity. Besides, hydraulic fractures are frequently arrested by these natural fractures/faults, leading to overstimulation along them and reducing fracture system’s complexity. In this study, 3D integrated fracture-hit mitigation and fracture complexity enhancement technology is proposed to minimize the impact of fracture hits, avoid overstimulation along natural fractures/faults, and initiate fracture branches to increase fracture complexity. We first identify the stages with high risk based on geological interpretation data. Then, different sizes of proppants, degradable fibrous materials, temporary plugging agents, and the activators (specially-designed particles) are injected together to form a low-permeable interwoven structure with the help of viscosity-enhanced fracturing fluid. The plugging process involves four stages: (1) bridging, (2) bonding, (3) agglomeration, and (4) formation of the solid plugging pack. Real-time adjustment of fracturing fluid properties is conducted to satisfy the requirements the of plugging materials. Proppants, fibrous materials, temporary plugging agents, activators, and high-viscosity liquid completely plug the tips of multi-scale fractures, realizing 3D plugging of the whole SRV. Fracture branches are then created with the increase of net pressure. Indoor plugging capacity tests show that the plugging pressure difference between the two sides of the temporary plugging pack varies from 2.5 MPa to over 33 MPa, depending on injected materials’ fraction combination. Finally, by using a high-efficiency gel breaker, only proppants exist after degradation of the interwoven structure and the gelatinous plugging pack, leading to high conductivity at the fracture tips. This technology has been successfully applied to deep shale gas formations in the Southern Sichuan Basin. During fracturing operations, the pressure increments of adjacent wells are all less than 5.64 MPa. Compared with previous observations, some of the pressure increments are reduced by over 50% under similar stimulation intensity. Microseismic monitoring results indicate that the event locations of the treated stage are well-confined within a certain stimulated area, mitigating inter-well communications. The event density within the SRV is larger compared with that of adjacent stages. Production logging results show that the stages using this technology even provide higher contribution to well production compared with adjacent stimulated stages. This technology can be further improved and rolled out to other types of reservoirs for fracture hit mitigation.

records.title: 2023 SPE Diversity and Inclusion Survey: Driving Equality in the Energy Industry
records.summary: Abstract An SPEi survey was launched in May 2023 to determine the status of Diversity and Inclusion (D&I) in the energy industry from the workforce perspective. Besides, survey results were compared with the results of a similar survey launched in 2020. The survey consisted of seven demographics, fifteen multiple-choice and five open-ended questions overall similar to the questions from the 2020 survey. A few additions aimed to capture changes in the workplace due to the pandemic and the ongoing energy transition. The proposal was reviewed and approved by the SPE D&I committee. SPE Marketing Research Group submitted the survey to SPE members and non-members located worldwide. The survey was also promoted on social media to increase its reach. The responses were analyzed with the help of charts and tables that summarized key findings. More than 900 responses were received from all over the world. 74% were men, 21% women, 1% non-binary and 4% preferred not to answer the gender question. Most of the participants were from North America (58%) and Western Europe (12%), followed by Asia (8%), South America (8%) and Africa (7%). 96% of the respondents held college degrees. Their ages were 26-35 years old (12%), 36-45 years old (20%), 46-55 years old (17%), 56-65 years old (21%) and older than 66 years old (23%). 58% worked for upstream, 14% for oil field services and equipment and 13% were consultants. Most professionals have positive perceptions about the industry's benefits, work environment, and contributions to the energy transition, top conditions to recruit and retain younger generations. Most respondents prefer to work virtually or part time from home. Women consider that they face gender biases at work and that their careers are limited by negativity or discrimination by management. While some participants express skepticism or opposition to D&I initiatives, the majority emphasize the importance of creating an inclusive work environment. Hiring, assignments and promotions were supported based on merit regardless of differences or merit without using quotas to benefit minorities. The understanding of women and men about important D&I topics differs. For example, majority of women perceive that, even today, they are not treated equally at work, while majority of men perceive that everyone is treated equally. D&I has matured to include not only aspects of identity (gender, race) but also aspects of the value and benefits obtained by promoting diversity of thoughts, making merit-based decisions, challenging biases, and fostering equal opportunities for all employees. The different opinions that women and men have expressed in the survey illustrate how organizations can be nurtured by the presence of diverse individuals that bring their unique perspectives and contributions for long-term success.
